summary: A country in northern South America, the only country in South America with English as its official language; it was a British colony, and in recent years its economy has grown rapidly because of offshore oil discoveries.

ranking.name: Protestantism (Pentecostal, Anglican, etc.)
ranking.description: In 1814 Britain acquired Guyana from the Dutch, and in 1831 it was merged into British Guiana. In 1808 the London Missionary Society sent missionaries to preach to slaves on the plantations, and after the Demerara slave rebellion of 1823 the missionary John Smith was accused of incitement and died in prison, drawing attention to the British abolition movement. The Anglican, Methodist and other churches took root among residents of African descent, and in recent decades Pentecostal churches have grown rapidly, making Protestantism the largest religious group.

ranking.name: Hinduism
ranking.description: After Britain abolished slavery in 1834, planters, to replenish the labor force, brought about 240,000 indentured laborers from India in 1838–1917, most of them Hindus. Their descendants, Indo-Guyanese, are the country's largest ethnic group, and both Diwali and Phagwah (Holi) are public holidays. But after the 1960s large numbers of Indo-Guyanese emigrated to North America, causing the proportion of Hindus to fall.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: From 1835 large numbers of immigrants from Madeira in Portugal arrived as indentured laborers; they were Catholics and later mostly became merchants. In addition, Jesuits preached to Amerindians in the Rupununi region in the south, so Catholicism also has quite a few followers in indigenous communities.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam was brought mainly by the Muslims among the indentured laborers who came from India in 1838–1917, making up a little over a tenth of Indian immigrants. They built mosques near the plantations, and Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha are now public holidays too, making Guyana one of the countries with the most diverse religious holidays.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The non-religious are few in number, mainly young people in the capital Georgetown. Religious activity is vigorous in Guyanese society, and the festivals of different religions are valued nationwide, so the proportion of people who identify with no religion at all is very low.

religion.background: Guyana was originally the land of Amerindians; from the 17th century the Dutch set up plantations and trafficked African slaves, and after 1814 the British took over and brought the Anglican Church and other Protestant denominations. After abolition in 1834, the British colonial authorities brought indentured laborers from India, the Portuguese island of Madeira and China, making Guyana a society of great religious and ethnic diversity: people of African descent are mostly Christians, while Indo-Guyanese are mostly Hindus or Muslims. After independence in 1966, the festivals of Christianity, Hinduism and Islam were all made public holidays, reflecting the character of coexisting religions.

ranking.name: English (including Guyanese Creole English)
ranking.description: Guyana is the only country in South America with English as its official language. The Dutch colonized here in the 17th–18th centuries, and after the British took over in 1814 English became the language of administration and education. African slaves on the plantations and later Indian laborers developed "Guyanese Creole" (Creolese), based on English and absorbing Dutch, African and Indian vocabulary; it is the everyday spoken language of the whole population, while Standard English is used on formal occasions.

ranking.name: Spanish
ranking.description: Spanish speakers come mainly from neighboring Venezuela. After the collapse of Venezuela's economy in 2015, large numbers of migrants crossed the border into Guyana, and, together with the long-standing territorial dispute between the two countries over their border, Spanish has become increasingly common in border areas and among immigrant communities in the capital.

language.history: The indigenous peoples of Guyana speak languages of families such as Arawakan and Cariban, which are still used in the interior today. Dutch colonization in the 17th century brought the Dutch language, and many place names (such as Essequibo and Demerara) still preserve Dutch traces. After 1814 British rule made English the official language, and African slaves and Indian, Chinese and Portuguese indentured laborers on the plantations gradually shifted to an English-based Creole. After independence in 1966 English retained its status as the official language, and Guyana therefore has close ties with the English-speaking Caribbean countries.

ranking.name: Pepperpot
ranking.description: Beef, pork or mutton is stewed for a long time with a black sauce refined from cassava (cassareep), cinnamon, chili and brown sugar, producing a deep black, rich sauce.
ranking.history: Pepperpot originates with the Amerindians of Guyana, who used "cassareep", boiled from bitter cassava juice, to cook and preserve meat; this sauce has a preservative effect, and in the past a pot of stew could be reheated repeatedly and kept for days. In the colonial period people of African descent and other groups also adopted the dish, forming today's version. It is regarded as Guyana's national dish and is traditionally eaten with family on Christmas morning, with thick slices of bread.

ranking.name: Cook-up rice
ranking.description: Rice cooked in one pot with beans such as black-eyed peas, coconut milk and chicken, beef or salted meat, with herbs and chili added; the flavor is rich.
ranking.history: Cook-up rice comes from the food tradition of Afro-Guyanese; the name means "cooked up in one pot", and it was originally a frugal dish of leftover meat and beans cooked with rice, while the coconut milk reflects the produce of the Caribbean coast. It is common at Saturday family lunches and is also a traditional dish for Guyanese welcoming the New Year, when many families cook a big pot on New Year's Day to share with relatives and friends.

ranking.name: Roti
ranking.description: A soft flatbread made of flour, cooked on a griddle and clapped to bring out its layers, often eaten with curried chicken, potato or pumpkin.
ranking.history: Roti was brought by the indentured laborers who came to Guyana from India in 1838–1917 and is the everyday staple of Indo-Guyanese households. Over more than a hundred years it has become a food of all Guyanese, appearing with curry at restaurants, weddings and religious ceremonies. The Guyanese version of roti is especially soft and layered, and is called "buss-up-shut" (oil roti), because after being torn apart it looks like a torn shirt.

ranking.name: Phulourie
ranking.description: A batter of split yellow pea flour with spices is fried into small round balls, crisp outside and soft inside, eaten with a sweet-and-sour mango or tamarind sauce.
ranking.history: Phulourie comes from the food tradition of Indian indentured laborers; fried snacks made of pulses are very common in northern India, and after migration to the Caribbean a local version developed. It is a common snack in Indo-Guyanese households on occasions such as Diwali, Phagwah and weddings, and is also sold on the streets and in snack shops, becoming a snack loved regardless of ethnic group.

ranking.name: Dhal puri
ranking.description: Dough is filled with a cooked, ground yellow split pea filling seasoned with cumin and garlic, rolled out into a thin flatbread and cooked on a griddle, and eaten with curry.
ranking.history: Dhal puri originates from similar foods of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh in northern India, the homeland of most Indian indentured laborers. After migration to the Caribbean the bread developed into a larger, thinner version, becoming a distinctive food of Indo-Caribbean people. Because it takes more work to make, it often appears at Hindu ceremonies, weddings and festival feasts.
